title: Sharing the Trend Following Pie - Systematic Investor 299

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Sharing the Trend Following Pie - Systematic Investor 299.docx

speakers: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged, trend-following background)
Andrew Beer (co-manager of DBMF managed futures replication ETF)
summary: Weekly Systematic Investor episode (June 2024). Beer and Kaastrup-Larsen discuss why short selling stopped paying, why trend followers are the only true shorts, how replication handles lag and reversals, Pivotal Path data showing managed futures are only ~6% of hedge fund assets despite zero equity correlation and 340bp alpha, and why advisors/allocators do not buy them (narrative, anxiety, fees, ETF economics).

coverage.note: small talk: US politics, weather, European elections; nothing actionable
real yields pre/post 2009 and debt-service/bond vigilante risk
near-term macro forecasts no better than coin toss; macro models crisis; short sellers closing
trend followers as the only true shorts; asymmetry and timing risk of single-stock shorting
capacity limits and selection bias in short selling; two dominant investor types
trend following edge vs value buyers, 2022 alpha, timing CTA entry
dollar cost averaging into CTAs, trend index performance, replication lag and Nov 2023 reversal
head fakes and window-based replication; speed of exits trade-off
faster exit research vs Sharpe, replication adaptivity, skis pointing the same way
stop prevention is costly; hedge fund fees; Pivotal Path data intro
managed futures share of hedge fund assets, correlation, beta, alpha, Sharpe
allocator incentives and why institutions do not adopt replication
why managed futures has not grown: smoothing and nomenclature (private equity analogy)
narrative gap vs equity long short, crisis alpha framing, 60/40 to 50/30/20
advisor communication, beacon of green, sister anecdote start
macro as worry-less strategy, advisor emotions, concern about fee race
low-cost airline analogy, low fees not necessarily good
ETF cost structure, fees and manager economics, new entrants
wealth management walled gardens, pricing floor, close
outro; nothing actionable

completeness_estimate: 0.82 - first reader caught the core arguments on short selling, replication lag, Pivotal Path statistics and the adoption barriers (about 56 of roughly 68 ideas); missed the June 2024 macro views, the trend-window lag mechanics, reversal persistence, fee-differential and data-sample details

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: before 2009 so before really the GFC real yields in the US was about 2% above inflation
claims.claim: Pre-2009 US real yields were about 2% above inflation but since then about 0.25% or less; the past 10-15 years may be the abnormal period, so rates dropping at the long end is not assured and many portfolios are not positioned for normal real yields.
claims.direction: rates higher for longer at the long end
claims.testable: yes - real yield series are public

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: then the bond V Vigilantes will come out and basically with their feet and and the bond markets collapse
claims.claim: With real yields near 2% and 4.5-5.5% on 10- and 30-year bonds, heavily indebted governments risk Truss-style moments where excess stimulus triggers a bond market collapse until the government steps in.
claims.direction: bond yields up on fiscal slippage

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: these near-term macro predictions that have are really no better than a toin than a coin toss
claims.claim: Market expectations for the 2-year yield a year ahead are always wrong (chart of rate forecasts as filaments around the actual line), so near-term macro predictions are no better than a coin toss.
claims.testable: yes - forecast error vs realised yields can be measured

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I think there is a existential crisis in a lot of macroeconomic modeling
claims.claim: Macro models failed to anticipate the 2010s (no fiscal restraint yet no inflation in 2014-15), so people have no good replacement.
claims.testable: partly - forecast accuracy of models is testable

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: who are generally always talking their own books in some way shape or form
claims.claim: Media rotate commentators depending on the latest print and each commentator is talking his own book, adding noise to macro commentary.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: every time Trend following is pronounced dead people redeem and then you know hey ho 6 months later they have a great run
claims.claim: Investors redeem after trend following is declared dead, then it posts a strong run about six months later; short sellers closing (Chanos etc.) after a long bull market may come just before shorts are most needed.
claims.testable: yes - flows vs subsequent CTA returns can be tested

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we can truly go short when markets point in that direction
claims.claim: Trend followers have no long bias so they were genuinely short bonds in 2022-2024, whereas bearish macro managers often held other positions instead of shorting bonds; trend followers may be the only true short sellers left.
claims.testable: partly - compare stated views to actual positions

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you get it unbelievably perfect timing and everything else you make 50% you know if you get the timing wrong or or other things you know you lose 200%
claims.claim: Single-stock short selling has a horribly asymmetric payoff: at best about 50% gain while losses can reach 200%, so the odds are stacked against it.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the answer is we just got to take over all like you know 70% premium to the stock
claims.claim: Even correct fundamental shorts can fail through takeover premiums or prolonged mispricing (Chanos story), so being right on fundamentals does not make a short work.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: as you get bigger the the the short constraints or the capacity constraints on the short side um are are are become much much more difficult
claims.claim: A hedge fund can run a concentrated long book but a short book must be diversified, so beyond a certain size shorting individual stocks cannot generate alpha (Tesla wiped out shorts; Melvin/GameStop).

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it was just selection bias right you you get 50 guys who are doing it and you're looking around you're GNA there a couple of guys who going to look like like Geniuses
claims.claim: Short-selling alpha seen in selected funds (Einhorn on Lehman, Chanos on Enron) vanished the moment allocators invested, because of selection bias and a halo effect.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we as Trend followers believe that markets move up and down
claims.claim: Trend followers earn from broad bear markets in diversified sectors without needing single-stock shorts, which helps portfolios.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: is dominated by two kinds of people
claims.claim: Investing is dominated by slow-moving long-only asset allocation models and by mean-reversion/intrinsic-value stock pickers, so few participants trade momentum.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: something like Trend following which will short after it's already gone down
claims.claim: Fundamental pickers buy after declines (long holding periods, belief the market mispriced) while trend following shorts more as the market goes from 100 to 80, a competitive advantage because it ignores intrinsic value.
claims.testable: yes - behaviour of trend vs value in declines

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the magnitude the hundreds of billions of dollars of of Alpha can be generated for a period of time
claims.claim: Trend following alpha comes from being the one group built to exploit large trends: in 2022 hundreds of billions of alpha were available because most of the investing world could not act.
claims.conditions: in persistent macro trends such as 2022

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you're trying to time this and you're part you know try to pick the bottom or something honestly don't
claims.claim: Do not try to time entry into trend following; most investors set a 3-5% allocation after months of study and timing is too random.
claims.testable: partly - timing evidence for CTA entry could be studied

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: dial it in over over over three allocations you know do a third each quarter for the next three quarters
claims.claim: Phase into a 5% CTA allocation by thirds over three quarters (dollar cost averaging) to avoid entering at the worst point, as many investors did in 2022 before a bad 2023.
claims.testable: yes - phased vs lump-sum entry is testable

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if they're thinking about this as a 6mon trade I honestly say it's I don't think you should
claims.claim: Managed futures should be a long-term strategic allocation; as a six-month trade investors will be disappointed and leave.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own Trend barometer closed yesterday at 41 so it's kind of neutral to weak
claims.claim: June 2024 trend environment: his Trend barometer 41 (neutral to weak), uses short time frames and tracks the short-term traders index (+2.38% YTD) more than the longer-term SG Trend index (+9.21% YTD).
claims.indicator: Trend barometer; SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-term Traders indices

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: replication will always be a little bit slower than the underlying funds
claims.claim: Replication looks back about four weeks of data and so always lags the funds it tracks.
claims.indicator: replication of managed futures indices (four-week look-back)

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we've all collectively walked into a propeller
claims.claim: On 1 Nov 2023 Powell signalled the end of hikes and nearly everyone was short Treasuries; the sharp reversal hit all trend-followers and replicators at once.
claims.indicator: Treasury short positioning, SG CTA index
claims.conditions: at inflection points after a steady trend

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: empirically though a lot of the times that sharp move is a head fake
claims.claim: Sharp one- or two-day reversals often reverse; a slower window (17 old data points plus 3 new) therefore avoids some whipsaw even if it misses real reversals.
claims.conditions: after sudden risk-off events that fade
claims.testable: yes - head fake frequency is testable

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: guys like that also you know in in a period like 2022 they're also likely to underperform
claims.claim: Managers with fast exits get out earlier on reversals but are likely to underperform in sustained trend years like 2022; the choice depends on loss tolerance vs long-term returns.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I do see lower draw downs but I see I see also I see you know you're getting lower draw downs but you're adding a different kind of whipsaw risk
claims.claim: Faster exits and risk reduction in trend following lower drawdowns but add whipsaw risk and probably hurt the Sharpe ratio over time.
claims.testable: yes - testable on CTA index data

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: some of the changes we have made have certainly helped and improved our sharp ratio
claims.claim: We cannot know the counterfactual of unchanged models over 15 years; his own firm's changes did improve Sharpe.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you've got 11 skis pointing in the same direction
claims.claim: Replication hurts when whipsaw is a market-wide theme across many positions rather than one or two positions going wrong.
claims.conditions: when a macro theme drives many positions

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: what I always liked about replication is when you're when you're wrong you're never that wrong
claims.claim: Replication is adaptive because new data is always entering, so a wrong week is corrected the next (model unchanged since 2016).

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: so the idea that the dream is not that you have a stop loss is you have a stop prevention but but that's really costly and and you end up giving a lot for that
claims.claim: Predicting drawdowns in advance (stop prevention) is hard and expensive; the space's returns would suffer if everyone tried.

correction.issue: Second half misstates the point: Beer says that if the whole space found a way to predict drawdowns and exit early, a slower replication model would capture less of the space's returns (he is skeptical it can be done); he does not say the space's returns would suffer.
correction.fix: Predicting drawdowns in advance ('stop prevention' rather than a stop loss) is very hard and costly; if the space did learn to exit before drawdowns, a replicator that adapts only gradually would capture less of the space's returns, so Beer doubts it can be done.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: now hedge fund fees consume 80% of Alpha
claims.claim: Hedge fund fees take about 80% of alpha.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: hedge fund databases overall always have this incompleteness issue
claims.claim: Hedge fund indices miss large firms (Citadel, Wellington, sometimes Millennium), so Pivotal Path holdings data is the most complete.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: Futures represent uh about 6% of the assets
claims.claim: Pivotal Path shows managed futures are about 6% of hedge fund assets versus equity long/short 37% and multi-strat 20%, so institutions are ridiculously underinvested in managed futures.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: manage Futures is a correlation into two equities of zero
claims.claim: Correlation to equities: managed futures 0, multi-strat 0.5, equity long/short 0.75; betas 0, 0.1 and 0.3-0.4.
claims.indicator: correlation and beta to equities by category

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: manage F has 340 basis points per anom of alpha to an allocator in in stocks
claims.claim: Managed futures delivered 340bp per year alpha to an equity allocator, more than multi-strategy funds (280bp), while equity long/short added flat to slightly positive alpha.
claims.indicator: alpha vs equities, Pivotal Path categories
claims.conditions: Sept 2015 onward including the long winter

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you get 75% of the returns but doubl the all so you end up with a much lower sharp ratio
claims.claim: Managed futures give about 75% of multi-strat returns with double the volatility, hence a lower Sharpe despite the diversification and alpha.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we don't make for a typical person in that space whose job is to be a head fund allocator we don't make their life better
claims.claim: Replication does not help hedge fund allocators because their job and status are tied to evaluating hedge funds, so institutional adoption fails despite lower fees and better drawdowns.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: would I rather have something that got marked down five in that period of time
claims.claim: Private equity grew by selling smoothed marks to pension allocators who prefer a 5% markdown to a true 30-40% loss in front of an unsophisticated committee.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: managed Futures does not have an inherent positive connotation
claims.claim: Name matters for adoption: private equity and high yield sound good while managed futures causes anxiety.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they are armed with a narrative not just on the initial investment but how to manage it over time
claims.claim: Equity long/short managers can explain drawdowns (cheap stocks got cheaper), whereas managed futures lack a narrative, so allocators fear explaining a drawdown to the investment committee.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it gets people focused on the issue that youve described is should I buy it today or next month
claims.claim: Crisis alpha framing pushes investors to time purchases instead of holding managed futures permanently.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the world is going from 60 40 to 50 30 20
claims.claim: Portfolios are shifting from 60/40 to 50/30/20 and the 20% alternatives bucket is where managed futures compete with gold and TIPS.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: something's working when nothing else is working
claims.claim: A 5% managed futures allocation will not save a portfolio in a major bear market but helps at the margin as the green in a sea of red.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if the adviser doesn't think he can describe that $100,000 in a way that makes the person the other side feel warm and happy
claims.claim: Advisors will not allocate to a product they cannot explain simply to clients.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's a strategy that helps you to worry a little bit less about the world
claims.claim: Managed futures pitch to retail: macro investors treat world dislocations as opportunities, so a small allocation lets investors worry less.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if we make this about just getting it cheaper and cheaper and cheaper we're going to introduce we're going to end up with worse products
claims.claim: Concern that fee cutting turns CTA ETFs into the low-cost airline model, with less experienced and worse products.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: low fees is not necessarily good like lower fees and hedge fundes is not necessarily good
claims.claim: Low fees are not good if the product is worse; a hedge fund at 10 before / 6 after fees beats a cheap fund at 6 before / 3 after.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's going to cost 10 to 15 basis points to to to really run it
claims.claim: ETF fees will not fall to zero: running an ETF costs 10-15bp at scale plus marketing and platform costs, and DBMF at 85bp is in line with active ETFs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the managers certainly are not making more than a few basis points frankly
claims.claim: If a product charges about 80bp and costs are as high as stated, the manager earns only a few basis points.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the US wealth management business is a whole series of Walled Gardens
claims.claim: Pricing is held up by distribution gatekeepers (platforms want a cut, hedge fund channels profit from high fees), so ETF fees will not go to zero unless Vanguard decides otherwise.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the latest us unemployment numbers which are somewhat surprising for those who keep saying that interest rates are going to drop like a stone
claims.claim: June 2024 view: the strong US jobs report is further evidence against the claim that rates will fall sharply and inflation will quickly return to 2%, so he stays cautious on rate cuts.
claims.testable: partly - jobs surprise versus subsequent rate path

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it doesn't feel recession let's say um but two months from now I could be wrong
claims.claim: June 2024 non-quantitative view: the US economy does not feel like it is slowing much or entering recession (only pockets of weakness), held with low conviction.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I'm kind of Happy the number came in strong today because it's been you know I mean I think a lot of a lot of us have been positioned for you know a healthier inflationary environment
claims.claim: Managed-futures and trend managers were positioned in mid-2024 for a stronger-inflation, higher-yield environment (short bonds), so a strong data print helps their performance.
claims.direction: short bonds benefits from strong data
claims.testable: partly - CTA bond positioning versus data surprises

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: msci world as of last night up 1.3% in June up 10.12 for the year
claims.claim: Early-June 2024 scoreboard: BTOP50 and SG CTA both +7.2% YTD, SG Trend +9.21%, short-term traders +2.38% versus MSCI World +10.12% and S&P 500 +12.9%, i.e. trend followers lagged a strong equity market while bonds sold off after the jobs number.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, MSCI World, S&P 500 YTD returns

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it drops from 20 to 18 right okay so now your now your six-month window of time is 10 to 18 still pretty good
claims.claim: Window-return trend signals stay long through the first part of a reversal (10 to 20 then back to 18 still shows +80% over the window), so exits are inherently late; when a steady rise has every short, medium and long horizon long, the whole trend universe is all in and a reversal hits every horizon at once.
claims.direction: signals flip only after retracement deepens
claims.conditions: after a long steady trend with all lookbacks aligned
claims.testable: yes - signal lag after peaks can be simulated

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they would all get out a week after it starts and then avoid the difficulties of the next seven weeks as it continues
claims.claim: The Nov 2023 bond reversal hurt because it continued for about seven weeks, not because it happened; if managers could know a reversal would persist they would all exit within a week, but most sharp one-day moves are head fakes, so exit speed differs by manager (index CTAs with tight trip wires and vol controls de-risk fast, replicators miss it).
claims.conditions: reversals that continue rather than fake out
claims.testable: partly - fraction of sharp reversals that persist is measurable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: although Trend followers to a large extent have become longer term in terms of our look back periods and so on and so forth I think that that's I think pretty Universal uh across the space
claims.claim: Trend followers have broadly lengthened their lookback periods, and recent manager innovation has focused on reacting faster on the exit side (risk reduction on more than volatility).
claims.direction: longer entry lookbacks with faster risk-reduction exits

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I mean if you look at the manager today the last 10 years it's not3 even though we went through a difficult period of time but it's it's higher than that
claims.claim: The common view of trend following Sharpe (about 0.3 as the caption renders it) understates the last ten years of managers' realised Sharpe, which was higher even through the difficult period (caption garbled, treat the exact figure as uncertain).
claims.testable: yes - manager and index Sharpe ratios are measurable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I can give you a better return 3 to 400 basis points more because we have low cost
claims.claim: A low-cost replicator can deliver roughly 300-400bp more net return than a 1.5-and-10 fee structure for similar exposure, which is why it risks taking assets from incumbent managers rather than only growing the pie.
claims.testable: yes - fee differential versus tracking error

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I'm sure more more big Pension funds do internal Trend follow I'm I'm pretty sure of that but we don't see the those kind of numbers
claims.claim: Visible external CTA assets understate trend-following adoption because large pension funds likely run trend following in-house, although the data does not show it.
claims.testable: no - in-house assets are not observable

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: their manage Futures category has 58 funds in it whereas the stock CT index has 20
claims.claim: Method point: Pivotal Path's managed-futures category covers 58 funds against 20 in the SG CTA index and its data starts in September 2015, so the 340bp alpha estimate spans roughly nine years including the long winter and is a broader sample than a standard CTA index.
claims.indicator: Pivotal Path managed futures category (58 funds) vs SG CTA index (20)
claims.testable: yes - holdings data is the source

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: established it's already there they already have a longer track record so so people are going to come in they're going to say well okay we're kind of try to adapt part of that
claims.claim: In replication ETFs the market leader's track record is a moat: a pure copycat cannot win, so entrants adapt part of the model, add their own overlay and cut price, which fuels fee competition.
